title: A rolling deployment triggers a rebalance for every pod restart: why does it hurt more than expected and how do you fix it?
shortTitle: A rolling deployment triggers a rebalance for every pod restart: why does it hurt more than expected, and how do you fix it?

s1_definition.oneliner: Every pod stop and start is a separate membership change, and with eager rebalancing each one pauses the entire group, so a rolling deploy of N pods costs 2N stop-the-world pauses unless you switch to cooperative, sticky, and static-membership strategies.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Eager rebalance** -- the default protocol where on any membership change every consumer revokes all partitions and re-joins, causing a stop-the-world pause.
- **2N rebalances** -- a rolling deploy of N pods triggers roughly 2N stop-the-world rebalances (one per stop, one per start), each pausing the entire group.
- **Cooperative sticky assignor** -- consumers only revoke the specific partitions that actually need to move, keeping all other partitions consuming throughout.
- **Static group membership** -- giving each pod a stable `group.instance.id` lets the coordinator skip the rebalance when a pod restarts within the session timeout.
- **Stacking fixes** -- cooperative sticky removes most of the cost from unavoidable rebalances; static membership eliminates rebalances for quick restarts.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India has ten tellers at ten counters, and customers are split by account number. When the manager sends each teller for a coffee break one at a time, with the old rule every single time one teller leaves or comes back, all ten tellers close their counters, huddle in the back room, and re-divide the entire customer list from scratch. The fix is a smarter rule where only the affected counter is touched and the other nine keep serving.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
 Eager vs Cooperative Rolling Deploy
 ====================================

 Eager Rebalance (default):
 ─────────────────────────
  Pod 1 stops  → ALL consumers stop, revoke ALL partitions
                  ↓ reassign ↓ resume
  Pod 1 starts → ALL consumers stop, revoke ALL partitions
                  ↓ reassign ↓ resume
  Pod 2 stops  → ALL consumers stop, revoke ALL partitions
                  ↓ reassign ↓ resume
  ...repeat for every pod...
  Total: 2N stop-the-world pauses


 Cooperative Sticky + Static Membership:
 ───────────────────────────────────────
  Pod 1 stops  → static member, session timeout running
  Pod 1 starts → same instance.id, coordinator skips rebalance
                  ↓ zero pause
  Pod 2 stops  → static member, session timeout running
  Pod 2 starts → same instance.id, coordinator skips rebalance
                  ↓ zero pause
  ...repeat for every pod...
  Total: 0 rebalances (if restart < session timeout)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A rolling deployment hurts far more than expected because the default eager rebalance protocol is stop-the-world. Each pod stop and start triggers a separate rebalance where every consumer revokes all partitions, so a deploy of N pods costs roughly 2N full group pauses during which no partition is consumed.

The fix has two parts that stack. First, the cooperative sticky assignor ensures that only partitions needing to move are paused while everything else keeps consuming. Second, static group membership with a stable instance id per pod lets the coordinator skip the rebalance entirely when a pod restarts quickly.

In my National Bank of India settlement service, six consumer pods on twelve partitions caused visible lag spikes on every deploy. After switching to cooperative sticky plus static membership, deploys caused zero rebalances and latency stayed flat throughout.

Remember one sentence: switch to cooperative sticky assignor and static group membership so rolling deploys cause zero stop-the-world rebalances and partitions are never paused.

---

keyPoints: Eager rebalancing causes 2N stop-the-world pauses for a rolling deploy of N pods.
Cooperative sticky assignor pauses only the partitions that need to move, not the entire group.
Static group membership with group.instance.id lets the coordinator skip rebalance on quick restarts.
These two fixes stack: static membership for zero rebalances, cooperative sticky for minimal cost when rebalances occur.
Set session.timeout.ms to exceed pod restart time so static members are recognized on return.
The preStop hook should call consumer.close() for graceful group departure.
